derivations.claim: For each fixed coordinate $j$, apply [F2] with one-dimensional prior variance $C_0=\tau_j^2$, observation map $A=s_j$, and noise variance $\Gamma=\epsilon^2$. Then $AC_0A^T+\Gamma=s_j^2\tau_j^2+\epsilon^2>0$, and [F2] gives posterior mean $\tau_j^2s_jY_j/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=\lambda_jY_j/s_j$ and variance $\tau_j^2-\tau_j^4s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=v_j$.

For every finite coordinate set $J$, the prior/noise pairs indexed by $J$ are independent of the pairs outside $J$. Applying [F2] to the diagonal finite block gives the product of the scalar laws from step 1.1 as the conditional law of $\theta_J$ given $Y_J$; independence makes it the same conditional law given the full data. The product Gaussian law $Q_y=\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jy_j/s_j,v_j)$ exists on $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ by [F3]. On finite-coordinate cylinders its evaluations are Borel functions of $y$; the class of Borel sets $B$ for which $y\mapsto Q_y(B)$ is measurable is a Dynkin system containing the generating cylinder $\pi$-system, so [F6] makes $Q$ a probability kernel. The same finite-block conditional identity holds on data cylinders, and [F5] applied successively in the data and parameter coordinates extends it to all product-Borel events. Thus $Q_y$ is the prior-predictive conditional law on the product coordinate space.

Put $m_j(y)=\lambda_jy_j/s_j$ and $Y_0=\{y:\sum_jm_j(y)^2<\infty\}$. This is Borel because each $m_j$ is coordinate-measurable and $\ell^2=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\bigcap_{N\ge1}\{x:\sum_{j=1}^Nx_j^2\le k\}$. Since $v_j\le\tau_j^2$, [F7] gives $\int\sum_jx_j^2\,Q_y(dx)=\sum_j(m_j(y)^2+v_j)<\infty$ on $Y_0$, so $Q_y(\ell^2)=1$ there. Under the prior-predictive law, $\mathbb E m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2\tau_j^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=\lambda_j\tau_j^2\le\tau_j^2$; under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)=\lambda_j\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$ and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2\le(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\tau_j^2$. Applying [F7] to the partial sums shows $Y_0$ has full measure under both laws. Restrict $Q_y$ to $\ell^2$ on $Y_0$ and set it equal to $\delta_0$ outside $Y_0$; this is a posterior version on $\ell^2$ and is defined for fixed-truth-almost every observation.

For $y\in Y_0$, the product posterior has coordinate mean $m_j(y)$ and variance $v_j$, so its expected squared coordinate error is $(m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j$. The partial sums of these nonnegative errors increase to $\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$; [F7] therefore gives $\int\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid y)=\sum_j((m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j)$, with the value $+\infty$ allowed.

Under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger=-(1-\lambda_j)\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$. The noise has mean zero and variance one, so its cross term has expectation zero and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}(m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2=(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2$. The identity $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j$ gives $\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2$. Taking expectations in step 4.1 and applying [F7] to the nonnegative partial sums proves the displayed exact series identity.

For each fixed data sequence, apply [F8] to the posterior probability measure with $f(\theta)=\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$ and threshold $R^2>0$. This gives posterior tail mass at most $R^{-2}$ times the posterior second moment. Taking fixed-truth expectation and using step 5.1 yields the stated bound. If $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$, substitute $R=M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ to obtain expected tail mass at most $C/M_\epsilon^2\to0$ for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$; [F9] identifies $r_\epsilon$ as a posterior contraction rate.

derivations.claim: Let $H=\ell^2$ with standard basis $(e_j)$ and set $\tau_j^2=j^{-1-2\alpha}$. Each dyadic block $2^k\le j<2^{k+1}$ has at most $2^k$ terms, each at most $2^{-k(1+2\alpha)}$, so [F5] gives $\sum_j\tau_j^2\le\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-2\alpha k}<\infty$. Define $\Gamma e_j=\tau_j^2e_j$. It is positive and self-adjoint; its truncations $\Gamma_N$ have finite rank, and $\|\Gamma-\Gamma_N\|\le\sup_{j>N}\tau_j^2\le\sum_{j>N}\tau_j^2\to0$, so [F6] makes $\Gamma$ compact. The expansion $\Gamma x=\sum_j\langle x,\tau_j^2e_j\rangle e_j$ has nuclear sum $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$, so [F6] also makes it trace class. By [F7] there is a Borel centered Gaussian random element $G$ in $H$ with covariance $\Gamma$. For each finite coordinate vector, every linear projection is centered normal by [F7], hence it is jointly Gaussian by [F8]; its covariance matrix is diagonal with entries $\tau_j^2$. Repeatedly applying [F9] to the first coordinate and the remaining block proves that the coordinates are independent, and [F10] identifies their laws as $N(0,\tau_j^2)$. Thus the law of $G$ is the stated prior on $\ell^2$.

Put $d=1+2\alpha+2p$ and $J=\lceil\epsilon^{-2/d}\rceil$. Since $\epsilon^{-2/d}\ge1$, one has $\epsilon^{-2/d}\le J\le2\epsilon^{-2/d}$. The posterior variance satisfies $v_j\le\min\{j^{-1-2\alpha},\epsilon^2j^{2p}\}$. Therefore $\sum_{j\ge1}v_j\le\epsilon^2\sum_{j\le J}j^{2p}+\sum_{j>J}j^{-1-2\alpha}\le\epsilon^2J^{2p+1}+2J^{-2\alpha}\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-2\alpha k}\le C_{\alpha,p}\epsilon^{4\alpha/d}$. The finite sum has at most $J$ terms each at most $J^{2p}$; for the tail, the block $2^kJ<j\le2^{k+1}J$ has at most $2^{k+1}J$ terms, each at most $(2^kJ)^{-1-2\alpha}$.

Write $b_j=1-\lambda_j=\epsilon^2/(\epsilon^2+j^{-d})\le\min\{1,\epsilon^2j^d\}$. The ellipsoid condition gives $\sum_jb_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2\le L^2\sup_j b_j^2j^{-2\beta}$. For $j\le J$, this supremum is bounded by $\epsilon^4J^{2d-2\beta}$ when $\beta\le d$, and by $\epsilon^4$ when $\beta>d$. For $j>J$, it is at most $J^{-2\beta}$. The bounds on $J$ in step 1.2 give $\sum_jb_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2\le C_{\alpha,\beta,p,L}\epsilon^{\min\{4\beta/d,4\}}$. This treats the equality case $\beta=d$ in the first branch.

Since $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j\le1$, one has $v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2=v_j\lambda_j\le v_j$. The exact sum [F1] and steps 1.2–2.1 therefore give $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C_{\alpha,\beta,p,L}\epsilon^{4\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/d}$; here $4\alpha/d<4$. Setting $r_\epsilon=\epsilon^{2\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/d}$ makes the expected posterior tail outside $M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ at most $C/M_\epsilon^2$, which tends to zero for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$. By [F2], this is the stated contraction rate.

derivations.claim: Let $H=\ell^2$ with standard basis $(e_j)$ and set $\tau_j^2=e^{-2\alpha j}$. Since $e=\exp(1)$, real-power definition and logarithm inversion give $e^{-2\alpha}=\exp(-2\alpha)$; strict increase, positivity and $\exp(0)=1$ imply $0<e^{-2\alpha}<1$. By the exponent laws, $\tau_j^2=(e^{-2\alpha})^j$, so [F6] gives $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$. Define $\Gamma e_j=\tau_j^2e_j$. It is positive and self-adjoint; its truncations $\Gamma_N$ have finite rank, and $\|\Gamma-\Gamma_N\|\le\sup_{j>N}\tau_j^2\le\sum_{j>N}\tau_j^2\to0$, so [F7] makes $\Gamma$ compact. The expansion $\Gamma x=\sum_j\langle x,\tau_j^2e_j\rangle e_j$ has nuclear sum $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$, so [F7] also makes it trace class. By [F8] there is a Borel centered Gaussian random element $G$ in $H$ with covariance $\Gamma$. For each finite coordinate vector, every linear projection is centered normal by [F8], hence it is jointly Gaussian by [F9]; its covariance matrix is diagonal with entries $\tau_j^2$. Repeatedly applying [F10] to the first coordinate and the remaining block proves that the coordinates are independent, and [F11] identifies their laws as $N(0,\tau_j^2)$. Thus the law of $G$ is the stated prior on $\ell^2$.

Put $q=\alpha+p$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, let $J$ be the largest positive integer with $e^{qJ}\le1/\epsilon$. Since $q>0$, the exponential is increasing and unbounded, so $J$ exists and $J\to\infty$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. Maximality gives $e^{qJ}\le1/\epsilon<e^q e^{qJ}$, hence $e^{-q}/\epsilon<e^{qJ}\le1/\epsilon$. The posterior variance satisfies $v_j\le\min\{e^{-2\alpha j},\epsilon^2e^{2pj}\}$. Reversing the finite geometric sum for $j\le J$ and summing the tail gives $\sum_{j\ge1}v_j\le C_{\alpha,p}(\epsilon^2e^{2pJ}+e^{-2\alpha J})\le C'_{\alpha,p}\epsilon^{2\alpha/q}$. For the first term, $e^{2pJ}=(e^{qJ})^{2p/q}\le\epsilon^{-2p/q}$. For the second, $e^{qJ}>e^{-q}/\epsilon$ gives $e^{-2\alpha J}<e^{2\alpha}\epsilon^{2\alpha/q}$.

Write $b_j=1-\lambda_j=\epsilon^2/(\epsilon^2+e^{-2qj})\le\min\{1,\epsilon^2e^{2qj}\}$. The truth ellipsoid implies $\sum_jb_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2\le L^2\sup_j b_j^2e^{-2\beta j}$. For $j\le J$, this is bounded coordinatewise by $\epsilon^4e^{(4q-2\beta)j}$; its maximum is at $J$ if $\beta\le2q$, and then is at most $\epsilon^4(e^{qJ})^{4-2\beta/q}\le\epsilon^{2\beta/q}$. If $\beta>2q$, the exponent is negative and the maximum is at $j=1$, bounded by a constant times $\epsilon^4$. For $j>J$, the source weight gives $b_j^2e^{-2\beta j}\le e^{-2\beta J}=(e^{qJ})^{-2\beta/q}\le e^{2\beta}\epsilon^{2\beta/q}$. Thus the squared-bias term is at most $C_{\alpha,\beta,p,L}\epsilon^{\min\{2\beta/q,4\}}$.

Since $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j\le1$, one has $v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2=v_j\lambda_j\le v_j$. Combining [F1] with steps 1.2–2.1 gives $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C_{\alpha,\beta,p,L}\epsilon^{2\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/q}$: when $\beta\le\alpha$, the bias exponent is $2\beta/q$; when $\beta>\alpha$, the variance exponent $2\alpha/q<2$ dominates the bias bound, including the branch $\beta>2q$. Taking $r_\epsilon=\epsilon^{\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/q}$, [F1] bounds the expected tail outside $M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ by $C/M_\epsilon^2\to0$. By [F2], this is the claimed posterior contraction rate.

derivations.claim: The prior $\delta_0=N(0,0)$ is a proper centered Gaussian law. Under its prior-predictive joint law, $\theta=0$ almost surely, so for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and product-Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, $\mathbb P(\theta\in A,Y\in B)=\mathbf 1_A(0)\mathbb P_0^\epsilon(Y\in B)=\int_B\delta_0(A)\,\mathbb P_0^\epsilon(dy)$. Thus the constant kernel $y\mapsto\delta_0$ is a posterior version. The prior assigns zero mass to every ball centered at $e_1$ of radius less than $1$.

Under the fixed truth $e_1$, only the first data coordinate shifts. Relative to the prior-predictive data law, the one-coordinate normal density ratio is $L(y)=\exp\!\left(\frac{s_1y_1}{\epsilon^2}-\frac{s_1^2}{2\epsilon^2}\right)$, and it integrates to $1$ under the prior-predictive first-coordinate law. It is positive and finite for every $y$ by [F4]–[F6]. All remaining coordinates have identical independent laws. The two full product-Borel data laws therefore agree as finite measures on the generating cylinder $\pi$-system after weighting by $L$; [F5] extends the identity to all data events. Since $L>0$, the laws are equivalent, so the posterior version $\delta_0$ remains the same almost surely under the truth law.

For any candidate rate $r_\epsilon\to0$, take $M_\epsilon=r_\epsilon^{-1/2}$ for sufficiently small $\epsilon$. Then $M_\epsilon\to\infty$ and $M_\epsilon r_\epsilon=\sqrt{r_\epsilon}<1$ eventually. The posterior is concentrated at $0$, whose distance from $e_1$ is $1$, so its mass outside the radius-$M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ ball is exactly $1$ under the truth law. This violates [F7] and refutes the Statement. The example lies outside the positive-coordinate-variance hypotheses in [F2].
